Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 17, verse 1 (part 1 of 2):

He, glory be to Him, mentioned His servitude ('ubudiyyah) in the most noble of His station(s): the station of the Night Journey (al-Isra'), the station of the call (da'wah), and the station of challenge (tahaddi). In the station of the Night Journey He said: ﴿Glory be to He who took His servant by night﴾. He did not say "His Messenger" or "His prophet," indicating that he stood in this greatest station through the perfection of his servitude to his Lord.

In the station of the call He said: ﴿And when the servant of God stood up calling Him, they almost became around him a pressing crowd﴾.

In the station of challenge He said: ﴿And if you are in doubt about what We have sent down upon Our servant, then produce a surah like it﴾.

In the two Sahihs, in the hadith of the intercession and the prophets' declining it, and the words of the Messiah: "Go to Muhammad, a servant whom God has forgiven his past and future sins."

This indicates that he attained that greatest station through the perfection of his servitude to God and the perfection of God's forgiveness of him. And if servitude before God has this rank, His wisdom required that He settle Adam and his offspring in an abode where they might attain this degree through the perfection of their obedience to God, their drawing near to Him by what He loves, and their abandoning what they are accustomed to for His sake. This was part of the completion of His favor upon them and His kindness to them.

(Section)
The real meaning of ta'abbud (worship/servitude) is humiliation and submission before the Beloved. From it is the saying of them: "a paved path (tariq mu'abbad)," meaning a made-smooth one, which feet have made submissive. So the servant (al-'abd) is the one whom love and submission to his Beloved have humbled. For this reason, the most noble states and stations of the servant are in servitude, and there is no station more noble than it.

God, glory be to Him, mentioned the most honored of creation before Him and the most beloved to Him, His Messenger Muhammad ﷺ, by servitude in his most noble stations: the station of calling to Him, the station of challenge through prophethood, and the station of the Night Journey. He, glory be to Him, said: ﴿And when the servant of God stood up calling Him, they almost became around him a pressing crowd﴾ [al-Jinn: 19].
He said: ﴿And if you are in doubt about what We have sent down upon Our servant, then produce a surah like it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 23].
And He said: ﴿Glory be to He who took His servant by night from the Sacred Mosque to the Farthest Mosque﴾ [al-Isra': 1].

The hadith of the intercession: "Go to Muhammad, a servant whom God has forgiven his past and future sins." So he attained the station of intercession through the perfection of his servitude and the perfection of God's forgiveness of him. God, glory be to Him, created creation for worshipping Him alone with no partner, which is the most perfect kind of love together with the most perfect kind of submission. This is the reality of Islam and the religion (millah) of Abraham, from which whoever turns away has indeed made a fool of himself. He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And who would turn away from the religion of Abraham except one who makes a fool of himself? And We had chosen him in this world, and indeed he, in the Hereafter, is among the righteous. When his Lord said to him, "Submit," he said, "I have submitted to the Lord of the worlds." And Abraham instructed his sons in it, and so did Jacob, "O my sons, indeed God has chosen for you this religion, so do not die except as Muslims." Or were you witnesses when death approached Jacob, when he said to his sons, "What will you worship after me?" They said, "We will worship your God and the God of your fathers, Abraham, Ishmael, and Isaac, one God, and to Him we are Muslims"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 130-133].
For this reason the greatest sin before God is shirk.

(Benefit)
In His saying ﴿took by night His servant﴾, rather than "sent His servant" or "sent with him," there is an indication of his companionship with Him on the journey. The bi' here is for accompaniment, like the ha' in his saying: "he emigrated with his family" and "he traveled with his boy," and it is not for transitivity. For asra (to travel by night) is transitive by itself; one says sara bihi and asraahu. This is because that night journey was the greatest of his journeys, and travel relies on a companion. For this reason the traveler would say: "O God, You are the companion on the journey."

If it is said: this meaning is understood from the triliteral verb, so if it had been said sara bi-'abdihi, what is the benefit of combining the hamzah and the bi'? There are answers to this:
First: that both have the same meaning, and asra is intransitive like sara; one says sara Zayd and asra is the same. This is the view of a group.
Second: that asra is transitive and its object is omitted, meaning "he made his servant travel by night, [with] the Buraq." This is the view of Abu al-Qasim al-Suhayli and others. The first view is supported by the words of al-Siddiq: "We traveled the whole night, and until the sun was at its zenith on the next day."

The correct answer is that the triliteral verb transitive with bi' conveys two things:
One: the act proceeding from its doer.
Two: its accompaniment by what the bi' is attached to.
So when you say sirtu bi-Zayd and safartu bihi, you have performed the traveling, with Zayd accompanying you in it, as in the verse:
"And I traveled through the darkness with a group..."
And from the hadith: "He drew lots among his wives, and whichever one's lot came out, he went out with her."
As for the transitive with hamzah, it requires the act to fall upon the object only, as in His saying: ﴿God brought you out from the bellies of your mothers﴾ and ﴿So We brought them out from gardens and springs﴾ and their like. So when this transitive is combined with the hamzah, it conveys the act falling upon the object together with the accompaniment understood from the bi'. Had it been said with the triliteral, it would convey the meaning of sharing in its verbal noun, which is impossible; so reflect on it.

(Subtlety)
The honor of the Messenger of God ﷺ came as a surprise without prior appointment, so that he would bear no pain of waiting, and he would be surprised by the honor suddenly. Moses's honor (peace be upon him) came after waiting forty nights.

(Benefit)
The subjugation of the Buraq to carry the Messenger of God ﷺ in a single night over a distance of two months' journey, going and returning, is greater than the subjugation of the wind for Solomon over a distance of two months in one day, going and returning, for the wind is swift in motion, its nature being to hasten with what it carries; but in the case of the Buraq, the sign is greater.

(Benefit)
The angels' saying to the Prophet ﷺ on the night of the Isra': "Marhaban bihi" (welcome to him)
is a basis for the use of these expressions and what suits them at meeting, such as (ahlan wa sahlan, marhaban, karamah, khayr muqaddam, and ayman mawrid) and the like.
Only the word marhaban was used alone because the situation called for it, for tarhib (welcoming) means spaciousness, and he had arrived at spacious places; sahlan was not used because its meaning is "you have trodden an easy place," while the Prophet ﷺ was being carried up to the heavens.

(Benefit)
The Prophet ﷺ's saying about Joseph: "He was given half of beauty."
A group said that what is meant is that Joseph was given half the beauty that Muhammad was given; the Prophet ﷺ reached the utmost in beauty, and Joseph reached half of that utmost.
They said that what confirms this is what al-Tirmidhi narrated from the hadith of Qatadah from Anas, who said: "God did not send any prophet except with a handsome face and a beautiful voice, and your Prophet was the most handsome of them in face and the most beautiful in voice."
The apparent meaning is that Joseph, peace be upon him, was singled out among people by half of beauty, and all people share in the other half; so he was distinguished from them by his half alone. This is the apparent wording, and the definite article in "al-husn" is for the genus, not for a specific or known beauty peculiar to the Prophet ﷺ. I do not know what led them to depart from this to what they stated. The hadith of Anas does not contradict this; rather it indicates that the Prophet ﷺ was the most handsome of the prophets in face and the most beautiful in voice, and it does not follow from his being the most handsome in face that Joseph was not singled out among people by half of beauty while they shared the other half; the Prophet ﷺ would then have shared with Joseph in what Joseph was singled out for, and surpassed him with another beauty from the second half. And God knows best.

(Section)
He was taken by night, with his spirit and body ﷺ, to al-Masjid al-Aqsa; then he was made to ascend to above the heavens with his body and spirit to God, Mighty and Majestic, and He spoke to him and enjoined the prayers upon him. That occurred once; this is the most correct of the opinions.

It was said: it was a dream. It was also said: one says he was taken by night, and one does not say "awake" or "in a dream."

It was said: the journey to Bayt al-Maqdis was while awake, and to the heaven was in a dream.

It was said: the Night Journey occurred twice, once awake and once in a dream.

It was said: rather, he was taken by night three times, and this was after the mission (ba'th), by agreement.

As for what occurred in the hadith of Shurayk, that this was before he received revelation, this is among the errors of Shurayk, one of the eight, and his poor memory, in regard to the hadith of the Night Journey.

It was said: this was a night journey in a dream before the revelation.

As for the waking night journey, it was after prophethood.

It was said: rather, the revelation here is restricted, and is not the absolute revelation which is the beginning of prophethood; the meaning is: before he was revealed to concerning the matter of the Night Journey, so he was taken by night suddenly without prior notice. And God knows best.

[Another section: On the Isra' and the Mi'raj]
Then the Messenger of God ﷺ was taken by night, with his body according to the correct view, from al-Masjid al-Haram to Bayt al-Maqdis, riding the Buraq, in the company of Jibril, peace and blessings be upon them both. He descended there, led the prophets in prayer as imam, and tied the Buraq to the ring of the mosque's door.

It was said that he descended at Bayt Lahm and prayed there, but this is not reported from him at all.

"Then he was made to ascend that night from Bayt al-Maqdis to the lowest heaven. Jibril asked for it to be opened, and it was opened for him. There he saw Adam, the father of mankind, and he greeted him, and he returned the greeting, welcomed him, and affirmed his prophethood. God showed him the spirits of the blessed on his right, and the spirits of the wretched on his left. Then he was made to ascend to the second heaven and asked for it to be opened, and there he saw Yahya ibn Zakariyya and 'Isa ibn Maryam. He met them and greeted them; they returned the greeting, welcomed him, and affirmed his prophethood. Then he was made to ascend to the third heaven, and there he saw Yusuf, and he greeted him; he returned the greeting, welcomed him, and affirmed his prophethood. Then he was made to ascend to the fourth heaven, and there he saw Idris, and he greeted him, welcomed him, and affirmed his prophethood. Then he was made to ascend to the fifth heaven, and there he saw Harun ibn 'Imran, and he greeted him, welcomed him, and affirmed his prophethood. Then he was made to ascend to the sixth heaven, and there he met Musa ibn 'Imran, and he greeted him, welcomed him, and affirmed his prophethood. When he passed him, Musa wept. It was said to him: 'What makes you weep?' He said: 'I weep because a youth was sent after me, whose community will enter Paradise in greater number than my community.' Then he was made to ascend to the seventh heaven, and there he met Ibrahim, and he greeted him, welcomed him, and affirmed his prophethood. Then he was raised to Sidrat al-Muntaha, then the Bayt al-Ma'mur was raised for him, then he was made to ascend to the Majestic One, may His majesty be exalted, and he drew near to Him until he was ﴿at a distance of two bow-lengths or nearer, and He revealed to His servant what He revealed﴾ [al-Najm: 9], and He enjoined fifty prayers upon him. He returned until he passed Musa, who said to him: 'With what were you commanded?' He said: 'With fifty prayers.' He said: 'Indeed your community cannot bear that; return to your Lord and ask Him to lighten it for your community.' He turned to Jibril as if consulting him about that, and he gestured: yes, if you wish. So Jibril raised him until he brought him to the Majestic, Blessed and Exalted, while He was in His place. This is the wording of al-Bukhari in some of the chains. So He reduced ten from him. Then he descended until he passed Musa and informed him, and he said: 'Return to your Lord and ask Him to lighten it.' He kept going back and forth between Musa and God, Mighty and Majestic, until He made them five. Musa commanded him to return and ask for lightening; he said: 'I have become shy before my Lord, but I am content and submit.' When he had gone away, a caller called out: 'I have enforced My obligation and lightened it for My servants.'"

The Companions differed: did he see his Lord that night or not?

It is established from Ibn 'Abbas that he saw his Lord, and it is established from him that he said: "He saw Him with his heart (fu'ad)."

It is established from 'A'ishah and Ibn Mas'ud that they denied this, and they said: His saying ﴿And he had seen Him in another descent, at the Lote-tree of the utmost boundary﴾ [al-Najm: 13] refers only to Jibril.

It is established from Abu Dharr that he asked him: "Did you see your Lord?" He said: "There is light; how could I see Him?" That is: the light prevented me from seeing Him, as he said in another wording: "I saw light."

'Uthman ibn Sa'id al-Darimi related the consensus of the Companions that he did not see Him.

Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah, may God sanctify his spirit, said: Ibn 'Abbas's saying "he saw Him" is not contradictory to this, nor is his saying "with his heart." It is established from him that he said: "I saw my Lord, blessed and exalted," but this was not during the Isra'; it was in Medina, when he was delayed from them at the dawn prayer, and then he informed them about seeing his Lord, blessed and exalted, that night in his dream. On this Imam Ahmad, may God have mercy on him, built, and he said: "Yes, he saw Him in truth, for the visions of the prophets are true, without doubt." But Ahmad, may God have mercy on him, did not say that he saw Him with the eyes of his head while awake; whoever relates that from him has erred about him. Rather, he said once "he saw Him," and once he said "he saw Him with his heart," so two narrations are reported from him; a third is reported from the rephrasing of some of his companions: that he saw Him with the eyes of his head. These are Ahmad's texts, existing, and they contain nothing of that.

As for Ibn 'Abbas's saying that he saw Him with his heart twice: if his basis is the saying of God, ﴿The heart did not lie about what it saw﴾ [al-Najm: 11], then ﴿And he had seen Him in another descent﴾ [al-Najm: 13], and it is apparent that this is his basis, then it is established from the Prophet ﷺ that this seen one was Jibril, whom he saw twice in his form in which he was created. This saying of Ibn 'Abbas is the basis of Imam Ahmad's saying: "He saw Him with his heart." And God knows best.

**Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 17, verse 1 (part 2 of 2)**

As for His saying in Surat al-Najm: ﴿Then he approached and descended﴾ [53:8], it is other than the approach and descent in the story of the Isra' (the Night Journey). What is meant in (Surat al-Najm) is the approach and descent of Jibril (Gabriel), as ʿĀʾisha and Ibn Masʿūd said. The context also points to this, for He says: ﴿One mighty in power taught him﴾ [53:5], and this is Jibril: ﴿Possessor of strength; so he stood firm, while he was at the highest horizon. Then he approached and descended﴾ [53:6-8]. All the pronouns refer back to this mighty teacher, who is "possessor of strength" (dhū mirrah), meaning power, the one who stood firm at the highest horizon, and the one who approached and descended. So he came near to Muhammad ﷺ to within two bow-lengths or closer. As for the approach and descent in the hadith of the Isra', it is explicit that it is the approach and descent of the Lord, blessed and exalted. Surat al-Najm does not address that at all. Rather, it says that he saw Him in another descent at the Lote Tree of the Utmost Boundary (Sidrat al-Muntahā), and this is Jibril, whom Muhammad ﷺ saw in his true form twice: once on earth, and once at the Lote Tree of the Utmost Boundary. And Allah knows best.

[Section: On his ﷺ informing the Quraysh about the Isra']

When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ rose in the morning among his people, he informed them of what Allah, mighty and majestic, had shown him of His greatest signs. Their denial of him intensified, as did their harm to him and their eagerness against him. They asked him to describe Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem) to them, so Allah made it manifest to him until he saw it directly, and he began to inform them about its features, and they could not respond to him with anything.

He also informed them about their caravan on its journey and its return, and he told them about the time of its arrival and about the camel that would lead it. It happened as he had said, but this only increased them in aversion, and ﴿the wrongdoers refused everything but disbelief﴾ [17:99].

[Section: On the difference between saying the Isra' was with the spirit and saying the Isra' was a dream]

Ibn Isḥāq narrated from ʿĀʾisha and Muʿāwiya that they said: "The Isra' was only with his spirit, and his body was not lost." Something similar is reported from al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī. However, it should be understood that there is a great difference between saying "the Isra' was a dream" and saying "it was with his spirit without his body." ʿĀʾisha and Muʿāwiya did not say that it was a dream; they said: "He was taken by night with his spirit, and his body was not lost." The difference between the two matters is clear, for what the sleeper sees may be parables struck for known realities in perceptible forms. So he sees himself as though he was taken up to the heavens, or taken to Makkah and the regions of the earth, while his spirit has neither ascended nor gone anywhere. Rather, the angel of dreams has struck the example for him.

Those who said "the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was taken up" are of two groups: one group said he was taken up with his spirit and body, and the other group said he was taken up with his spirit without his body being lost. The latter did not mean that the ascension (miʿrāj) was a dream. They meant that the spirit itself was taken by night and ascended with it in reality, and it engaged in the kind of activity it engages in after separation from the body. Its state in that was like its state after separation in its ascent through the heavens, heaven by heaven, until it reaches the seventh heaven, where it stands before Allah, mighty and majestic, and He commands in it what He wills. Then it descends to the earth. What the Messenger of Allah ﷺ attained on the night of the Isra' is more complete than what the spirit attains at separation.

It is known that this is a matter beyond what the sleeper sees. But since the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was in a station of breaking customary norms, to the extent that his belly was split while he was alive and did not feel pain from it, his spirit, in its sanctified essence, was taken up in reality without death. Anyone other than him cannot attain the ascent to the heaven with the essence of his spirit except after death and separation. The prophets' spirits settled there only after separation from their bodies. But the spirit of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ ascended there while he was alive and then returned. After his death, it settled in the Highest Companion (al-Rafīq al-Aʿlā) with the spirits of the prophets, peace and blessings be upon them. Despite this, it still has oversight of the body, illumination, and connection to it, to the extent that it returns the greeting to whoever greets him. By this connection Musa was seen standing in prayer in his grave, and he was seen in the sixth heaven. It is known that Musa was not taken up from his grave and then returned to it. Rather, that was the station of his spirit and its settlement, while his grave is the station of his body and its settlement until the day when spirits return to their bodies. So he was seen praying in his grave, and he was seen in the sixth heaven. Likewise, the Prophet ﷺ is in the highest place in the Highest Companion, settled there, while his body in his tomb is not lost. When one greets him, Allah returns his spirit to him so that he may return the greeting, and he has not departed from the exalted assembly. Whoever's perception is dense and whose nature is coarse, and cannot grasp this, let him look at the sun in the height of its place, its connection and its effect on the earth, and the life of plants and animals by it. This is so, and the matter of the spirit is above this, for it has its own matter, and bodies have their own matter. This fire remains in its place while its heat affects a body far from it, although the bond and connection between the spirit and the body is stronger, more complete and more perfect than that. So the matter of the spirit is higher than that and subtler.

*He said, in verse:*
"Say to the inflamed eyes: beware lest you look
at the radiance of the sun; so veil yourself from the darkness of nights."

**Section**

Mūsā ibn ʿUqba narrated from al-Zuhrī: "The spirit of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was taken up to Bayt al-Maqdis and to the heaven one year before his emigration to Madina." Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr and others said: "Between the Isra' and the Hijra there was one year and two months," and the statement is concluded.

The Isra' happened once. It was said that it happened twice: once while awake and once in a dream. The proponents of this view seem to have wanted to reconcile the hadith of Sharīk, with his saying "then I awoke," with all the other narrations. Some said it happened twice: once before the revelation, based on Sharīk's words in his hadith, "and that was before he was revealed to," and once after the revelation, as all the other hadiths indicate. Some said it happened three times: once before the revelation and twice after it. All of this is confusion, and it is the method of the weak Literalists (Ẓāhiriyya) among the transmitters, who, whenever they find in the story a wording that differs from the context of some narrations, make it a separate occurrence. Whenever the narrations conflict for them, they multiply the events. The correct position, held by the leading authorities of transmission, is that the Isra' happened once, in Makkah, after the prophetic mission began.

How strange it is that these people claimed it happened multiple times. How could they suppose that each time the prayer was prescribed as fifty, then he went back and forth between his Lord and Musa until it became five, then He said: "I have confirmed My obligation and lightened it for My servants," and then he repeated it the second time to fifty, and then reduced it by tens? The memorizers of hadith have criticized Sharīk for wording errors in the hadith of the Isra'. Muslim cited the chain-supported portion of it and then said: "He advanced and delayed, added and omitted, and did not narrate the hadith in order." May Allah have mercy on him, for he did well.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 17, verse 3:

Ibn al-Mubarak said, from Shibl, from Abu Najih, from Mujahid, regarding His words, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, he was a grateful servant﴾.

He said: "He never ate anything without praising Allah for it, never drank any drink without praising Allah for it, and never seized anything (with his hand) without praising Allah for it. So Allah praised him: Indeed, he was a grateful servant."

Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: "When Noah ate, he said, 'All praise is for Allah.' When he drank, he said, 'All praise is for Allah.' When he dressed, he said, 'All praise is for Allah.' When he rode, he said, 'All praise is for Allah.' So Allah named him a grateful servant."

Ibn Abi al-Dunya said: "It has reached me from some of the wise (hukama') who said: If Allah did not punish for disobedience to Him, it would still be fitting that one not disobey Him in gratitude for His blessing."

Ibn al-Qayyim said, commenting on surah 17, verse 12:

And the Most High said: ﴿It is He who made the sun a radiance and the moon a light, and determined for it stations, that you might know the number of years and the reckoning. Allah did not create that except in truth. He details the signs for a people who know.﴾

In the moon and the determining of its stations are signs and wisdoms that are not hidden from those who reflect. His wisdom, glorified is He, in His governance required that He vary the measures of the night and the day, so that they are never permanently equal, nor longer than they are, nor shorter. Rather, their equality and the taking of one from the other came in accordance with wisdom, so that in a place where one of them is extremely short there is no animal or plant, like the place that the sun never rises upon nor sets upon. Had the day been the length of a hundred hours or more, or the night likewise, the benefits that Allah arranged through this measure of night and day would have been nullified.

Then consider the wisdom in the illumination of the moon and the stars in the darkness of the night. For although there is a need for darkness for the stillness of animals and the coolness of the air, the benefit did not require that the night be one unbroken, pitch-black darkness with no light in it, in which no work at all could be done. People sometimes need to work at night, because time is tight for them during the day and because of the intense heat in the daytime. So they need to work at night by the light of the moon, such as plowing the land, cutting crops, and other things. Thus the light of the moon at night was made a help to people for these tasks. And a small portion of light was placed in the stars so that they would fill the place of the moon when it is absent. The stars were made an adornment of the sky, landmarks by which one is guided in the darkness of land and sea, and clear proofs of the Creator, the All-Knowing, and other wisdoms by which this world is ordered.

The sun was made to remain in one unchanging state, neither increasing nor decreasing, so that the wisdom intended from it would not be nullified. The moon was made to be in a state that admits increase and decrease, so that the wisdom intended from its being thus would not be nullified. In its light there is a cooling and a hardening effect that corresponds to the heating and dissolving effect in the light of the sun, so that the benefit is ordered and the wisdom of this heating and cooling is completed.

Reflect also on the divine wisdom in making the wandering planets and their stations appear in some years and be hidden in others. For if they appeared constantly, or were constantly hidden, the wisdom intended from them would be lost. Just as wisdom required that some of them appear and some be hidden, so they do not all appear at once nor all vanish at once; rather, what is apparent stands in for what is hidden in indicating [the Creator]. And He made some of them apparent, never hidden at all, like the raised markers by which people are guided on unknown roads in land and sea: they look at them whenever they wish and are guided by them wherever they wish. Thus both matters came in accordance with wisdom.

Then consider the state of the stars and the variation of their courses. One group of them does not leave its positions in the sphere and does not move except together, like a single army. Another group is free, moving through the zodiacal signs and diverging in its course, so each one of them travels two different motions: one general, moving with the sphere toward the west, and another particular to itself, toward the east. It has two different motions, in accordance with wisdom. This is among the greatest indications of the Chooser, the All-Knowing, the All-Wise, and of the perfection of His knowledge, power, and wisdom.

Consider how this sphere, with its sun, moon, stars, and zodiac, turns over this world with this great, swift, continuous rotation, by a precise determination that neither increases, nor decreases, nor deviates from its order. Rather it is the determination of the Almighty, the All-Knowing, as the Most High indicated that this determination proceeds from the perfection of His might and knowledge, when He said: ﴿And the sun runs on to a resting place for it. That is the determination of the Almighty, the All-Knowing.﴾ [Ya-Sin: 38].

That is, whatever comes to him of good and evil as his omen is bound to his neck. The Arabs say, "Its omen (al-ta'ir) ran for him with such-and-such, of good and evil." Abu 'Ubayda said: "Al-ta'ir, in their usage, means fortune (al-hazz), which the common people call al-bakht (luck). They say, 'This one's omen flies for so-and-so,' meaning it comes to him." I say: from this is the hadith, "So Uthman ibn Maz'un flew for us," meaning it fell to us by lot, when the Ansar drew lots over the lodging of the Muhajirun with them. And in the hadith of Ruwayfi' ibn Thabit: "To the point that one of us would have fall to him the arrowhead and the feathers, and another the shaft," meaning it came to him through partnership in the booty.

It has been said regarding His saying ﴿And every person We have fastened his omen to his neck﴾ that the omen here is the deed. This was said by al-Farra'.

This includes a refutation of those who deny predestination (al-Qadariyya). The neck was singled out from among the parts of the body because it is the place of the collar that a person wears around his neck, from which he cannot free himself. From this one says, "The sin of this is on your neck," and "Do such-and-such, and its sin is on my neck." The Arabs say, "Its necklace is like the necklace of the dove," and "This is a noose (rabaqa) on his neck." It is reported from al-Hasan ibn Adam: "Look, for you a record that, when it is sent, is hung around your neck." They singled out the neck for this because it is the place of the necklace and the amulet. Their use of hanging charms on it is common, just as the hands are singled out for mention in such expressions as ﴿for what your hands have earned﴾ and ﴿for what your hands have sent forth﴾ and the like.

(Section)

Ibn Jarir said: "'And every person We have fastened to his neck what has been decreed for him, that he will do, and what he will come to, whether wretchedness or happiness, by his deed; he does not part from it.'" This is what people have said about the verse: that it is what came to him of wretchedness and happiness, and what came from him of deed. Then he (Ibn Jarir) related from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "His omen is his deed, and what has been determined for him; it stays with him wherever he is, and departs with him wherever he departs." Likewise Ibn Juraij, Qatada and Mujahid said: "It is his deed." Mujahid added: "and what has been written for him."

Qatada also said: "His happiness and his wretchedness are by his deed."

Ibn Jarir said: "If someone asks, 'How did He say, We have fastened his omen to his neck, if the matter is as you describe, and He did not say on his hands or his feet or any other part of the body?' It is said: the neck is the place of marks, the place of necklaces and collars, and other things that adorn or disgrace." So the speech of the Arabs attributes the things that cling to the bodies to the necks, just as they ascribe the offenses of the body's limbs to the hand. They say, "for what his hands have earned," even if what dragged him into it was his tongue or his private parts. Likewise His saying: ﴿We have fastened his omen to his neck﴾.

Al-Farra' said: "The omen, in their meaning, is the deed."

Al-Azhari said: "The basis of this is that when God, glorified is He, created Adam, He knew the obedient of his descendants and the disobedient, and He recorded what He knew of them all, and decreed the happiness of whom He knew to be obedient and the wretchedness of whom He knew to be disobedient. So the omen of each one was what he would come to at his creation and origination."

As for His saying ﴿on his neck﴾, Abu Ishaq said: "One only says of a thing that clings, 'This is on the neck of so-and-so,' meaning its clinging to him is like the clinging of a necklace from among what is worn on the neck." Abu 'Ali said: "Similar to this is their saying, 'I collared you with such-and-such, and I necklaced you with such-and-such,' meaning I turned it toward you and made it cling to you. And from this: 'The sultan entrusted him with such-and-such,' meaning the governorship became something that clings to him, in the place of the necklace and the collar."

It has been said: "He singled out the neck only because his deed is either good or bad, and that is among what adorns or disgraces, like jewelry or the shackle, so it was attributed to the necks."

The Qadariyya (those who deny predestination) said: "His fastening that to him means marking him with it and placing a sign by which the angels know that he is happy or wretched; the statement is about him, not that He fastened the deed to him and made it cling to him."

The People of the Sunna (Ahl al-Sunna) said: "This is a well-known method of yours in distorting words from their places, which you have followed regarding the body, nature, and intellect. The people of the language do not recognize this, it contradicts the literal sense of the wording, and it differs from what the most knowledgeable of the Ummah in the Qur'an explained. Nothing like what you say is reported from any one of the early generations of the Ummah at all, and no one other than you has explained the verse this way. Nor is it correct to read the verse this way, for the statement about him and the sign and mark only occurred after his omen, which clung to him from his deed. When that omen clung to him and never left him, He informed about him by it, and it became a sign and mark upon him. We have shown you the sayings of the leaders of guidance and the early generations of the Ummah about the omen, so show us your saying from any one of them who said it before you. Every sect of the people of innovation drags the Qur'an toward its innovations and misguidance and interprets it according to its doctrines and opinions, but the Qur'an is free of that. And success is from God."

(Fasl/Lata'if) A subtle point.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Whoever is guided, it is only for his own soul that he is guided; and whoever goes astray, it is only against it that he goes astray. No bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another. And We would never punish until We sent a messenger﴾.

So He, glory be to Him, ruled for His enemies with four judgments, which are the utmost of justice and wisdom:

The first: that the guidance of the servants through faith and righteous deeds is for their own souls, not for others.

The second: that their going astray, through the loss of that and their falling short of it, is against their own souls, not against others.

The third: that no one is held accountable for the sin of another.

The fourth: that He does not punish anyone except after establishing the proof against him through His messengers. So reflect on what is contained within these four judgments of His wisdom, justice and grace, and on the refutation of the people of delusion and false hopes, and of the people of ignorance of Allah, His names and His attributes.

(Section: On the difference between a muqallid who was able to attain knowledge and recognise the truth but turned away from it, and a muqallid who was not able to do so in any way)

Indeed, in this station there must be a detailed explanation by which the difficulty is removed, namely the difference between a muqallid who was able to attain knowledge and recognise the truth but turned away from it, and a muqallid who was not able to do so in any way. Both categories exist in reality. The one who was able but turned away is one who neglected and abandoned what was obligatory upon him; he has no excuse before Allah. As for the one incapable of asking and of knowledge, who is not able to attain knowledge in any way, they are also of two kinds. One of them desires guidance, prefers it, loves it, but is unable to reach it or to seek it because there is no one to guide him; his ruling is the ruling of those in the interval between prophets (ahl al-fatarat) and those to whom the call has not reached. The second is one who is averse, has no desire (for truth), and does not entertain any thought other than what he is upon. The first says: "O Lord, if I knew a religion better than what I am upon, I would have adhered to it and abandoned what I am upon, but I know nothing other than what I am upon and I am not able to reach anything else; this is the utmost of my effort and the limit of my knowledge."

The second is content with what he is upon, does not prefer anything over it, his soul does not seek anything else, and there is no difference in his view between his state of incapacity and his state of capacity. Both are incapable, but this one must not be equated with the first because of the difference between them.

The first is like one who sought the religion in the interval and did not attain it, then turned away from it after exhausting his effort in seeking it, out of incapacity and ignorance. The second is like one who never sought it, but died in his polytheism, even though if he had sought it he would have been unable to reach it. Thus there is a difference between the incapacity of the seeker and the incapacity of the averse.

So reflect on this point. Allah judges between His servants on the Day of Resurrection with His judgment and justice, and He does not punish anyone except those upon whom the proof has been established through the messengers. This is definitively established in general concerning all creation. As for whether a specific individual, Zayd or 'Amr, has had the proof established upon him or not, this is something one cannot intervene between Allah and His servants about. Rather, the obligation upon the servant is to believe that everyone who follows a religion other than the religion of Islam is a disbeliever, and that Allah, glorified and exalted, does not punish anyone except after the proof has been established upon him through the Messenger.

This is the general principle; the specific determination is left to the knowledge of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and His judgment in this matter pertains to the rulings of reward and punishment. As for the rulings of this world, they follow the apparent state of affairs: the children of disbelievers and their insane are disbelievers in worldly rulings, and they have the ruling of their guardians.

With this detailed explanation the difficulty in this matter is removed.

This is based on four principles:

The first: that Allah, glorified and exalted, does not punish anyone except after the proof has been established upon him, as He said: ﴿And We would never punish until We sent a messenger﴾ [al-Isra: 15]. He, exalted, also said: ﴿Messengers as bringers of good news and warners, so that people would have no argument against Allah after the messengers﴾ [al-Nisa: 165]. He, exalted, also said: ﴿Every time a company is cast into it, its keepers will ask them, "Did there not come to you a warner?" They will say, "Yes, indeed a warner came to us, but we denied and said, 'Allah has not sent down anything"'﴾ [al-Mulk: 8-9]. He, exalted, also said: ﴿So they will acknowledge their sin. So away with the companions of the Blaze﴾ [al-Mulk: 11]. He, exalted, also said: ﴿O assembly of jinn and mankind, did there not come to you messengers from among you, relating to you My verses and warning you of the meeting of this your Day?" They will say, "We bear witness against ourselves." The worldly life deceived them, and they will bear witness against themselves that they had been disbelievers﴾ [al-An'am: 130]. This is abundant in the Qur'an: it informs that He only punishes the one to whom the messenger came and upon whom the proof was established, the sinner who acknowledges his sin. He also said: ﴿And We did not wrong them, but they were the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 76]. The wrongdoer is one who knew what the messenger brought or was able to know it. As for one who had no report of the messenger at all, and was not able to know it in any way and was incapable of that, how can it be said that he is a wrongdoer?

The second principle: punishment is deserved for two reasons. One is turning away from the proof and not desiring knowledge of it and of what it requires. The second is obstinacy against it after it has been established and abandoning the desire to act upon what it requires. The first is the disbelief of aversion, and the second is the disbelief of obstinacy. As for the disbelief of ignorance where the proof has not been established and one is not able to know it, this is what Allah has negated punishment for, until the proof of the messengers is established.

The third principle: the establishment of the proof differs according to times, places and persons. The proof of Allah may be established upon disbelievers in one era and not in another, in one region and not in another, just as it may be established upon one person and not another, either due to lack of intellect and discernment, as with the child and the insane, or due to lack of understanding, as with one who does not comprehend the address and no interpreter was present to translate for him. Such a person is in the position of the deaf man who hears nothing and cannot understand, and he is one of the four who will argue with Allah on the Day of Resurrection, as mentioned earlier in the hadith of al-Aswad and Abu Hurayrah and others.

The fourth principle: the actions of Allah, glorified and exalted, follow His wisdom, from which He never deviates, and they are intended for their praiseworthy end and their commendable consequences.

This principle is the foundation of the discussion regarding these categories, upon which we build, together with receiving their rulings from the texts of the Book and the Sunnah, not from the opinions and intellects of men. The discussion of these categories cannot be counted, except by one who knows what is in the books of people and has examined the statements of the sects on this subject, and stops at the limit of their levels and the end of their boldness. And Allah is the One who grants success to rectitude, who guides to right direction.

As for one who does not affirm wisdom or causation, and reduces the matter to pure will which favours one of two like things over the other without a preponderant cause, he has relieved himself of this difficult station and of storming the great obstacles of these issues, and has placed them all under His saying: ﴿He is not questioned about what He does, but they will be questioned﴾ [al-Anbiya: 23]. He is the doer of what He wills. Allah has spoken truly, and He is the most truthful of speakers: ﴿He is not questioned about what He does﴾, because of the perfection of His wisdom, knowledge, and His placing of things in their proper places, and that there is no defect, futility or corruption in His actions for which He would be questioned as a created being is questioned. He is the doer of what He wills, but He does not will to do except what is good, beneficial, merciful and wise. He does not do evil, corruption or injustice, nor anything contrary to the requirements of His wisdom, owing to the perfection of His names and attributes. He is the Self-Sufficient, the Praiseworthy, the All-Knowing, the All-Wise.

(Section)

His saying: ﴿And when We intend to destroy a city, We command its affluent ones, and they commit sin therein﴾

This is a command of divine decree (amr taqdiri kawni), not a command of religious legislation (amr dini shar'i), for Allah does not command immorality. The meaning is: We decreed that and determined it. A group said, however, that it is a religious command, and the meaning is: We commanded them to obey, but they opposed Us and transgressed. The first view is more correct, because of the following points.

First: supplying a hidden element (idmar) departs from the original state, so one should not resort to it unless the sentence cannot be made sound without it.

Second: that requires two hidden elements: "We commanded them to obey Us," and then "they opposed Us" or "they disobeyed Us," or the like.

Third: what follows the fa' (fa') in this construction is the very thing commanded, as when you say: "I commanded him, so he did it," "I commanded him, so he stood up," "I commanded him, so he rode." The listener understands nothing other than this.

Fourth: He, glorified is He, made the cause of the destruction of the city His aforementioned command. It is known that His command to obedience and monotheism cannot be the cause of destruction; rather it is a cause of salvation and success.

If it is said: Is the command to obedience, together with the transgression, the cause of destruction?

It is answered: This is refuted by the fifth point, namely that this command is not restricted to the affluent; rather He, glorified is He, commands obedience to Him and to the following of His messengers, both the affluent and others. So it is not valid to restrict the command to obedience to the affluent.

Clarifying this is the sixth point: if the command were to obedience, it would be the very sending of His messengers to them. It is known that it is not fitting to say: "We sent Our messengers to its affluent ones, and they transgressed therein," for if the sending were only to the affluent, those beyond them would say: "He did not send to us."

Seventh: Allah's, glorified is He, intention to destroy the city occurs only after the sending of messengers to them and their denial of them. Otherwise, before that, He does not intend their destruction, because they are excused by their heedlessness and by the message not having reached them. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿That is because your Lord would never destroy the cities unjustly while their people are unaware﴾.

So when He sends the messengers and they deny them, He intends its destruction, and commands its leaders and affluent ones with a command that is kawni qadari (of decree), not shar'i dini (of religious law), to commit transgression in the city. Its people then gather in denying them, and its leaders transgress; then the command of Allah comes to it, and His word of destruction is realized upon it. The point here is to mention both the kawni and the dini command. Of the religious kind is His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah commands justice and good conduct﴾, and His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah commands you to render trusts to their owners﴾, and there are many such.

(Section: on the term "command")

It is of two kinds: the command of creation (amr takwin) and the command of legislation (amr tashri'), and the second may be disobeyed and opposed, unlike the first.

So His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when We intend to destroy a city, We command its affluent ones, and they commit sin therein﴾ does not contradict His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not command immorality﴾.

There is no need to strain by supposing the meaning "We commanded its affluent ones to obey, but they disobeyed Us and transgressed therein." Rather the command here is a command of creation and decree, not a command of legislation, for several reasons:

One: what is customary in such a construction is that what follows the fa' is the thing commanded, as you say: "I commanded him, so he stood," and "I commanded him, so he ate," just as if the verb were explicitly stated, as in His saying: ﴿And when We said to the angels: Prostrate to Adam, so they prostrated﴾, and as you say: "I called him, so he came," and His saying: ﴿On the Day He calls you, and you respond with His praise﴾.

Two: the command to obedience is not specific to the affluent, so it is not valid to interpret the verse as that, and the mention of the affluent loses its point; for all those sent to are commanded to obey, so the command to the affluent cannot be the cause of the destruction of all of them.

Three: this wondrous arrangement and marvellous construction requires that what follows the fa' be consequent upon what precedes it, as an effect follows its cause and a caused thing follows its cause. Do you not see that transgression is the cause of the word being realized against them, and the realization of the word against them is the cause of their annihilation? Likewise the command is the cause of their transgression and necessitates it, and that is the command of creation, not of legislation.

Four: His, glorified is He, intention to destroy them occurred only after their disobedience and opposition to His messengers. Their disobedience and opposition had already preceded, so Allah intended to destroy them and punished them by decreeing upon them the deeds with which their destruction becomes certain.

If it is said: Their earlier disobedience is the cause of their destruction, so what is the benefit of His saying: ﴿We commanded its affluent ones, and they committed sin therein﴾, when the transgression had already occurred from them?

It is answered: Although earlier disobedience is its cause, the destruction may be delayed from it and is not certain, as is the established custom of the Lord, exalted is He, in His creation: their destruction is not made certain by their sins. So when He intends to destroy them, and it must be, He brings about another cause with which destruction becomes certain. Do you not see that Thamud were not destroyed for their earlier disbelief until He brought forth the she-camel for them, and they hamstrung her, and then they were destroyed. The people of Pharaoh were not destroyed for their earlier disbelief in Moses until He showed them the successive signs, and their rebellion and obstinacy became firm, and then they were destroyed. Likewise, when He intended the destruction of the people of Lot, He sent the angels to Lot in the form of guests, and they sought them out for the immorality, attacked Lot and threatened him. Likewise, all nations: when Allah intends their destruction, He brings about for them a rebellion and aggression which seizes them in its wake, and this is His custom with His servants, in general and in particular. The servant disobeys Him while He forbears toward him and does not hasten to punish him; then when He intends to seize him, He appoints for him a deed by which to seize him, in addition to his earlier deeds. So the observer supposes that He seized him by that deed alone, but that is not so; rather the word was realized against him through that deed while it was before that

not realized against them by their earlier deeds, since they did what required the establishing of the right against them, but the Judge of judges had not decreed it, nor had the judgment been executed. Then, when they did after that what established the Lord's wrath against them, He executed His judgment upon them and enforced it. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿So when they angered Us, We took vengeance upon them﴾.

They had, before that, angered Him by disobeying His messenger, but His wrath had not settled and become firm upon them, since it was about to be removed by their faith. When He despaired of their faith, the wrath became fixed and firm, and the punishment came. This place is among the secrets of the Qur'an and the secrets of the divine decree, and the servant's reflection upon it is among the most beneficial things for him, for he does not know which of the sins is the one that makes his punishment certain, so that after it one would not say: "And Allah is the Helper."

**(A Noble Benefit Concerning Divine Decree)**

Whoever has a will, and Allah commands a servant who has a will, then if He grants him success (tawfiq) and wills for Himself to help him and inspire him to do what He has commanded, [the servant does it]. But if He forsakes him and leaves him to his will and his self, and he is of this (ḥathītha, the base, unrefined nature), he chooses only what his self and disposition desire. He, insofar as he is a human being, desires nothing but that. For this reason Allah has censured him in His Book for this ḥathītha, and He has praised him only for a matter additional to that ḥathītha, namely being a Muslim, a believer, patient, a doer of good, grateful, God-fearing, righteous, and the like.

This is a matter additional to the mere fact of his being human and having a sound will. But the mere soundness of the will does not suffice unless it is supported by a decree additional to that, which is tawfiq, just as mere soundness of the eye for perception does not suffice for seeing unless another cause occurs, namely a light separate from it.

Ibn al-Qayyim's commentary on surah 17, verse 22:

For the polytheist hopes through his association (with God) to gain victory at times, and praise and commendation at other times. So God, glory be to Him, informs that his aim is turned back upon him, and he attains only abandonment and blame.

The point is that these two aspects apply to the created being, and their opposites apply to the Creator, glory be to Him.

So the righteousness of the heart, its happiness and its success, lie in worshipping God, exalted is He, and seeking help from Him. Its ruin, its misery, and its harm, both immediate and deferred, lie in worshipping the created being and seeking help from him.

(A benefit)

The greatest of people in abandonment is one who attaches himself to other than God. What he loses of his welfare, his happiness and his success is greater than what he gains from the one he attaches himself to, and that one is subject to decline and loss. The example of one who attaches himself to other than God is like that of one who seeks shade from heat and cold in the house of the spider, the weakest of houses.

In sum, the foundation of polytheism and its base, upon which attachment to other than God is built, brings blame and abandonment upon its adherent, as God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Do not make with God another god, lest you sit condemned and forsaken﴾.

Condemned, with no one to praise you; forsaken, with no one to help you. For some people may be overpowered yet praised, like one who was overcome by falsehood; some may be blamed yet victorious, like one who was overpowered and dominated by falsehood; and some may be praised and victorious, like one who was established and held power by right. The polytheist who attaches himself to other than God falls into the worst of the four categories: he is neither praised nor victorious.

[Section: Acting on analogy (qiyas) is embedded in human nature]

From the words of the Exalted, ﴿So do not say to them, "Uff"﴾, I understood that what is intended is a prohibition of all kinds of harm, by speech and by deed, even if no other texts have come prohibiting harm in general. For if a man spat in the faces of his parents and beat them with a sandal, and then said, "I did not say to them 'uff'," people would regard him as utterly foolish, ignorant, and stupid, merely for distinguishing between the prohibited saying of "uff" and this act, before another prohibition had reached him. To deny this is to be obstinate against reason, understanding, and natural disposition.

Whoever knows the intent of a speaker through one of the indicators, it is obligatory to follow his intent, since words are not sought for their own sake; rather, they are indicators by which the speaker's intent is inferred. So when his intent becomes apparent and clear by any means, acting on what it requires is obligatory, whether it is by gesture, by writing, by a sign, by a rational indication, by a contextual circumstance, by a habit of his that is consistently maintained and never broken, or from the requirement of his perfection and the perfection of his names and attributes, and that it is impossible for him to intend what is known to be corrupt or to leave aside what is certainly beneficial. It is also inferred that his wanting a like case follows from his wanting its counterpart, its equal, and its similar, and that his disliking a thing follows from his disliking its like, its counterpart, and what resembles it. Thus the one who knows Him, His wisdom, and His attributes is certain that He wills this, dislikes that, loves this, and hates that.

And you find that one who has a great devotion to the school and opinions of a certain man—how does he understand his intent from his conduct and positions? He reports about him that he issues a legal ruling in such-and-such a way and holds such-and-such a view, and that he does not hold such-and-such or adopt it, on the basis of what is not explicitly found in his speech. The entire body of followers of the imams stands in exactly this same relation to their imams.

[Section: The Difference Between Moderation (iqtisad) and Miserliness (shuhh)]

As for the difference between moderation (al-iqtisad) and miserliness (al-shuhh): moderation is a praiseworthy disposition that arises from two qualities, justice ('adl) and wisdom (hikmah). By justice, one is balanced in withholding and in giving, and by wisdom, one places each of them in its proper place that befits it. From the two of them arises moderation, which is a middle course between two blameworthy extremes, as God the Exalted said: ﴿And do not make your hand chained to your neck, nor extend it completely outstretched, lest you sit reproached and destitute﴾.

God the Exalted also said: ﴿And those who, when they spend, are neither extravagant nor stingy, but are ever a moderate position between that﴾.

And God the Exalted said: ﴿Eat and drink, but do not be excessive﴾.

As for miserliness: it is a blameworthy disposition that arises from bad opinion (of God) and weakness of the soul, and it is nourished by the promises of Satan until it becomes panic (hala'). Hala' is extreme greed for a thing and being overcome by evil towards it, from which arises withholding it from giving and anxiety at losing it, as God the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, mankind was created anxious. When evil touches him, he is distressed; and when good touches him, he is withholding﴾.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 17, verse 32 (part 1 of 2):

He informed of its foulness in itself, for it is an ugliness whose repugnance has reached such a height that its foulness is established in minds, even among many animals. As al-Bukhari mentioned in his Sahih, from Amr ibn Maymun al-Awdi, who said: "I saw in the Jahiliyyah (the period of ignorance before Islam) a male monkey commit zina (unlawful intercourse) with a female monkey, so the monkeys gathered around the two of them and stoned them until they died."

Then He informed of its end result, that it is "evil as a way" (﴿saa sabeelan﴾), for it is a path of ruin, destruction and poverty in this world, and of punishment, disgrace and retribution in the Hereafter.

Since marrying the wives of one's fathers is among the worst of it, He singled it out for additional condemnation, saying: ﴿Indeed, it was an abomination and hatred, and evil as a way﴾ [An-Nisa: 22].

He made the success of the servant depend on guarding his private parts from it, so there is no path to success without that. He said: ﴿Certainly the believers have succeeded, those who are humbly submissive in their prayer, and those who turn away from ill speech, and those who are active in zakah, and those who guard their private parts, except from their wives or those whom their right hands possess, for indeed they are not blameworthy. But whoever seeks beyond that, then it is those who are the transgressors﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 1-7], up to His saying.

This contains three matters: that whoever does not guard his private parts is not among the successful, that he is among the blameworthy, and among the transgressors. So he has missed success, deserved the name of transgression, and fallen into blame. Thus, enduring the pain of desire and its struggle is easier than some of that.

Similar to this is that He condemned man, and that he was created anxious, not patient in good fortune or in misfortune. Rather, when good touches him he withholds and is stingy, and when evil touches him he panics. Except for those He excepted after that from among the saved of His creation, and He mentioned them: ﴿And those who guard their private parts, except from their wives or those whom their right hands possess, for indeed they are not blameworthy. But whoever seeks beyond that, then it is those who are the transgressors﴾ [Al-Ma'arij: 29-31].

So Allah the Exalted commanded His Prophet to order the believers to lower their gaze and guard their private parts, and to inform them that He is Witness over their deeds and aware of them: ﴿He knows the treachery of the eyes and what the breasts conceal﴾ [Ghafir: 19].

Since the beginning of this is from the direction of the sight, the command to lower it was placed before guarding the private parts, for incidents begin from the sight, just as the bulk of a fire comes from a tiny spark. So there is a glance, then a passing thought, then a step, then a sin.

For this reason it was said: whoever guards these four has secured his religion: the glances (al-lahazat), the passing thoughts (al-khatarat), the utterances (al-lafazat), and the steps (al-khutuwat).

So it is fitting for the servant to be the gatekeeper of his own self over these four gates, and to remain stationed on their frontiers, for through them the enemy enters upon him, roams through the homes and destroys whatever is high with complete destruction.

(Chapter: On committing the two forbidden paths and what they lead to of corruptions and pains)

It is fitting for every intelligent person not to take a path until he knows its safety, its dangers, and what that path leads to of safety or destruction. These two paths (zina and sodomy) are the ruin of the earlier and later generations, and in them are such dangers and destructions as they contain, and they lead their companion to the most evil ends and the worst places of perdition. For this reason Allah the Exalted made the path of zina the worst of paths, and He said: ﴿And do not approach zina. Indeed, it is an abomination and evil as a way﴾.

If this is the path of zina, then how about the path of sodomy (liwat), whose one act is equal in sin and punishment to multiples of zina, and multiples of multiples, as you will come to know, God willing.

As for the path of zina, it is the worst path, and the abode of its people is in the furnace, the worst abode, and their souls' resting place in the barzakh (the intermediate state) is in an oven of fire, its flame reaching them from beneath them. When the flame reaches them they cry out and rise, then return to their place, and they remain thus until the Day of Resurrection, as the Prophet (ﷺ) saw them in his dream, and the dreams of the prophets are revelation, without doubt. Al-Bukhari narrated in his Sahih from the hadith of Samurah ibn Jundub (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to often say to his companions: "Has any one of you seen a dream?" He said: So whoever Allah willed would relate to him what he would relate. And one morning he said: "Last night two visitors came to me, and they sent me off, and they said to me: 'Come along.' So I went along with them, and we came upon a man lying on his back, and another standing over him with a rock, and he was bringing the rock down upon his head and crushing his head, so the rock rolled away, and he would go after the rock and take it, and would not return until his head was restored as it was. Then he would return to him and do to him the same as he had done the first time." He said: "I said to them: 'Glory be to Allah, who are these two?'" He said: "They said to me: 'Go on, go on.'" He said: "So we went on, and came upon a man lying on his back, and another standing over him with an iron hook, and he would come to one side of his face and tear his cheek to his nape, and his nostril to his nape, and his eye to his nape." He said: "And perhaps Abu Raja said: 'He would split' (fa-yashuqqu)." He said: "Then he would turn to the other side and do to it the same as he had done to the first side, and he would not finish with that side until that side was restored as it was. Then he would return to him and do the same as he had done the first time." He said: "I said: 'Glory be to Allah, who are these two?'" He said: "They said to me: 'Go on, go on.' So we went on, and came upon something like an oven, he said: I think he said, and in it there was a clamor and voices." He said: "So we looked into it, and in it were men and women, naked, and a flame would come to them from beneath them, and when that flame reached them they cried out." He said: "I said to them: 'Who are these?'" He said: "They said to me: 'Go on, go on.'" He said: "So we went on, and came upon a river, I think he said, red like blood, and in the river was a man swimming, and on the bank of the river was a man who had gathered many stones beside him, and that swimmer would swim as much as he swims, then come to the one who had gathered the stones beside him, and he would open his mouth for him and he would feed him a stone, so he would go off swimming, then return to him, and every time he returned he would open his mouth for him and feed him a stone." He said: "I said to them: 'Who are these two?'" He said: "They said to me: 'Go on, go on.'" He said: "So we went on, and came upon a man of hideous appearance, the most hideous of the men you have seen, and beside him was a fire which he was stoking and running around." He said: "I said to them: 'What is this?'" He said: "They said to me: 'Go on, go on.' So we went on, and came upon a garden luxuriant, in it of every kind of spring (blossom), and between the midst of the garden was a very tall man, I could hardly see his head for its height in the sky, and around the man were children, the most numerous I had ever seen." He said: "I said to them: 'What is this, what are these?'" He said: "They said to me: 'Go on, go on.'" He said: "So we went on until we reached a great garden, I had never seen a garden greater than it nor more beautiful." He said: "They said to me: 'Ascend in it.'" He said: "So we ascended in it, until we reached a city built with bricks of gold and bricks of silver. We came to the gate of the city and asked for it to be opened, and it was opened for us, and we entered it, and men met us in it, half of their creation as the most beautiful of what you have seen, and half as the most ugly of what you have seen." He said: "They said to them: 'Go and plunge into that river.'" He said: "And there was a river flowing across, its water pure white, so they went and plunged into it, then returned to us, and that evil had left them, and they became in the most beautiful form." He said: "They said to me: 'This is the Garden of Eden, and that is your abode.'" He said: "So my sight rose upward, and there was a palace like a white cloud." He said: "They said to me: 'That is your abode.'" He said: "I said to them: 'May Allah bless you both, let me enter it.' They said: 'Not now, but you will enter it.'" He said: "I said to them: 'Indeed I have seen since last night a marvel, so what is this that I have seen?'" He said: "They said to me: 'As for us, we will inform you. As for the first man you came upon, whose head was being crushed with the rock, he is the man who takes the Qur'an and rejects it and sleeps through the obligatory prayer. As for the man you came upon whose cheek was being torn to his nape, and his nostril to his nape, and his eye to his nape, he is the man who goes out from his house and tells a lie that reaches the horizons. As for the naked men and women who were in the likeness of the oven, they are the fornicators (zunat) and the adulteresses (zawani).'"

Qutaybah ibn Sa'id said: Nuh ibn Qays narrated to us, he said: Abu Harun al-Abdi narrated to me, from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said:
"On the night I was taken on the Night Journey, I was taken to a great number of Allah's creatures: women hanging by their breasts, and some of them hanging by their feet, upside down, and they had screaming and wailing. I said: 'O Jibril, who are these?' He said: 'These are the ones who commit zina, and kill their children, and make for their husbands heirs from other than them.'"

Abu Nu'aym al-Fadl ibn Dukayn said: Abd al-Salam ibn Shaddad narrated to us, from Ghazwan ibn Jarir, from his father, that they discussed the fawahish (grave sins) in the presence of Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him). He said to them: "Do you know which zina is the greatest in the sight of Allah, may His praise be exalted?" They said: "O Commander of the Faithful, all of it is great." He said: "But I will inform you of the greatest zina in the sight of Allah, blessed and exalted: it is that a servant commits zina with the wife of a Muslim man, so he becomes a zani, and he has corrupted the Muslim man's wife for him." Then he said, at that point: "Indeed, on the Day of Resurrection, people will be sent a foul-smelling wind, until every pious and wicked person is harmed by it, until it reaches from them every extent, and it nearly holds the breaths of all people. A caller will call out to them, making them hear the voice, and say to them: 'Do you know what this wind is that has informed you?' They will say: 'By Allah, we do not know, except that it has reached us to every extent.' It will be said: 'Indeed, it is the wind of the private parts of the fornicators who met Allah with their zina and did not repent from it.' Then they will be turned away with it, and no Paradise or Fire will be mentioned at their turning away."

Al-Kharaiti said: Ali ibn Dawud al-Qantari narrated to us, Sa'id ibn Ufayr narrated to us, Muslim ibn Ali al-Khushani narrated to me, from Abu Abd al-Rahman, from al-A'mash, from Shaqiq, from Hudhayfah (may Allah be pleased with him), that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "O assembly of Muslims, beware of zina, for in it are six traits: three in this world and three in the Hereafter. As for the ones in this world: the loss of radiance, perpetual poverty, and shortness of life. As for the ones in the Hereafter: the wrath of Allah, a bad reckoning, and entry into the Fire."

It is reported from Anas ibn Malik (may Allah be pleased with him) that he said: "One who persists in zina is like a worshipper of idols." Some of them raised it (as a marfu' hadith), and this is more fitting to liken him to a worshipper of idols than a drunkard. In the Musnad and others, it is reported as marfu': "The drunkard is like a worshipper of idols." Indeed zina is greater than drinking wine. Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal (may Allah have mercy on him) said: "There is nothing greater after killing a soul than zina."

In the two Sahihs, from the hadith of Abu Wa'il, from Abdullah ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: I said: "O Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), which sin is greatest?" He said: "That you set up a rival to Allah while He created you." He said: "Then which?" He said: "That you kill your child for fear that he will share your food." He said: "Then which?" He said: "That you commit zina with the wife of your neighbor."

So Allah revealed in His Book a confirmation of that: ﴿And those who do not invoke with Allah another deity, nor kill the soul which Allah has forbidden except by right, nor commit zina—and whoever does that will meet a penalty﴾.

Qutaybah ibn Sa'id said: Ibn Lahi'ah narrated to us, from Ibn An'am, from a man, from Abdullah ibn Amr (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The one who commits zina with the wife of his neighbor, Allah will not look at him on the Day of Resurrection, nor purify him, and He will say to him: 'Enter the Fire with those who enter.'"

Sufyan ibn Uyaynah mentioned from Jami' ibn Shaddad, from Abu Wa'il, from Abdullah, who said: "When the measure is diminished, the rain is withheld; when zina becomes apparent, plague occurs; and when lying increases, bloodshed (al-harj) increases."

In the two Sahihs, from the hadith of al-A'mash, from Abu Hazim, from Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Three whom Allah will not speak to on the Day of Resurrection, nor look at them, nor purify them, and for them is a painful punishment: an old man who commits zina, a king who lies, and a poor arrogant man."

Sufyan al-Thawri mentioned from Mansur, from Rib'i ibn Hirash, from Abu Dhar (may Allah be pleased with him), that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said:
"Indeed Allah dislikes three: the old man who commits zina, the poor man who is conceited, and the stingy man who reminds of his favors."

Al-A'mash mentioned from Khaythamah, from Abu Abd al-Rahman, from Abdullah ibn Amr (may Allah be pleased with both of them), from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "The likeness of one who sits on the bed of a woman whose husband is absent is like one who is bitten by venomous snakes on the Day of Resurrection." Al-Mughayyabah is the woman whose husband has traveled for jihad, Hajj, or other than them.

In al-Nasa'i and others, from the hadith of Buraydah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "The sanctity of the wives of the mujahidin upon those who sit at home is like the sanctity of their mothers. And no man among those who sit at home who takes the place of a mujahid with his family, except that he will be made to stand before him on the Day of Resurrection, and it will be said: 'O so-and-so, this is so-and-so, so take from his good deeds whatever you wish.'" Then the Prophet (ﷺ) turned to his companions and said: "What do you think? He will leave him nothing of his good deeds." In another wording: "And if he deputizes him over his family and betrays him, it will be said on the Day of Resurrection: 'This one betrayed you regarding your family, so take from his good deeds whatever you wish.' So what do you think?"

The Qur'an-related commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 17, verse 32 (part 2 of 2):

It is enough to show the ugliness of fornication (zina) that Allah, glorified and exalted, in His perfect mercy, prescribed for it the most vile, the most severe and the most disgraceful of punishments, and commanded His believing servants to witness the punishment of its perpetrator. And among its ugliness is that Allah instilled it in some dumb animals that have no intellect, as al-Bukhari mentioned in his Sahih from ʿAmr ibn Maymun al-Awdi, who said: "I saw in the Jahiliyyah a monkey commit fornication with a female monkey, and the monkeys gathered around the two of them and stoned them until they died, and I was among those who stoned them."

(Section)

Fornication combines all the evil traits: little religion, loss of scrupulousness, corruption of manliness, and little jealousy. You will not find a fornicator who has scrupulousness, nor fulfillment of a covenant, nor truthfulness in speech, nor preservation of a friend, nor complete jealousy for his family. Treachery, lying, betrayal, little shame, lack of self-restraint, not disdaining violation of what is sacred, and the loss of jealousy from the heart are among its branches and its requirements.

Among its requirements is the wrath of the Lord by corrupting His sacred things and His dependents. If a man were to expose a king to such a thing, the king would receive him with the worst of receptions. Among them is the blackening and darkness of the face, and the gloom and loathing that overspread it, which appear to onlookers. Among them is the darkness of the heart and the extinguishing of its light, and this is what necessitates the extinguishing of the light of the face and the covering of darkness over it. Among them is constant poverty.

And in a report, Allah, the Exalted, says: "I am Allah, who destroys the tyrants and impoverishes the fornicators."

Among them is that it removes the esteem of its perpetrator and casts him down from the eyes of his Lord and from the eyes of His servants. Among them is that it strips him of the most beautiful names, which are the names of chastity, righteousness and justice, and gives him their opposites, such as the names of the wicked, the sinful, the adulterer and the traitor. Among them is that it strips him of the name of believer, as in the two Sahihs from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "A fornicator does not commit fornication while he is a believer." Thus he is stripped of the absolute name of faith, though he is not stripped of faith altogether.

Ja'far ibn Muhammad was asked about this hadith, so he drew a circle on the ground and said: "This is the circle of faith." Then he drew another circle outside it and said: "This is the circle of Islam." So when the servant commits fornication, he exits this one and does not exit that one.

The presence of some part of faith does not necessitate that one be called a believer, just as a man may have some part of knowledge and jurisprudence without being called a scholar or jurist, or have some part of courage and generosity without being called courageous or generous. Likewise he may have some piety without being called pious, and similar cases. The correct position is to apply the hadith according to its apparent meaning and not to interpret it in a way that contradicts its apparent meaning. And Allah knows best.

Among them is that he exposes himself to dwelling in the furnace in which the Prophet (ﷺ) saw the adulterers and adulteresses. Among them is that he loses the goodness with which Allah described the people of chastity, and exchanges it for the wickedness with which Allah described the fornicators, as Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Wicked women are for wicked men, and wicked men are for wicked women; and good women are for good men, and good men are for good women﴾.

Allah has forbidden Paradise to every wicked person, and has made it the abode of the good, and none enters it except the good. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Those whom the angels take in death while they are good, saying, "Peace be upon you; enter Paradise for what you used to do"﴾. And He said: ﴿And its keepers will say to them, "Peace be upon you; you have been good, so enter it to abide therein"﴾. They deserved the greeting of the angels and entry into Paradise only by their goodness, while fornicators are among the most wicked of creatures. Allah, glorified, has made Hell the abode of the wicked and its people.
